name: Carla Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll be honest, I nearly didn't come, because I thought you'd be from the company with a clipboard. But if it's independent, sure, I'll talk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Then let's start simple. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a development crew lead underground at a gold mine, about nine hundred metres down. I run a twin-boom jumbo, that's the drill rig that bores the holes for blasting new tunnel, and I look after a crew of five. Alarm at four, cage down at quarter past six, then it's drilling, charging, checking ground support, and arguing with the planning office about why the heading is behind. I love the drilling itself, getting a face pattern perfect, but the night shifts and the dust in your throat wear you out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the company spends money on gadgets before it fixes the ventilation on level twelve. If AI is just a fancier spreadsheet in the planning office, fine, it's not my fight. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the crew chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. I've watched them bring in tablets and tracking tags and every time it's sold as making us safer, and every time it ends up timing our tea breaks. If AI is a flop, that's one less thing for the bosses to clock us with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Finish my shift boss ticket, keep my crew in one piece, keep putting money aside. Dele and I want to put a deposit on a bigger place in town, and I'd keep pushing for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, because I've been saying it's hype for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a union delegate. Would AI come up at the union meetings at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would come up as surveillance, not as robots. The dispatch system already tracks every machine to the minute, and if they add AI on top, the question for me is who sees that data and what they use it for. That's a bargaining point, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in a year, if this is how it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still on the jumbo, still on the same crew, maybe running two headings instead of one. Still arguing with Kev in planning. I'd probably be on the union committee by then, because nobody else on our shift wants to do the paperwork.

S0.say: I'd tell people the company spends on gadgets before it fixes the basics like ventilation. If AI is just a fancier spreadsheet in the planning office, it's not her fight.
S0.think: Privately she'd be relieved, because every new tech rollout she has seen has ended up used to watch workers. She sees a flop as one less tool for managers to time her crew with.
S0.do: Keeps working the jumbo and finishes her shift boss ticket. Keeps saving towards a deposit on a bigger place in town with her partner, Dele, and takes on more union committee work.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, because she has called AI hype for years.
S0.quote: If AI is a flop, that's one less thing for the bosses to clock us with.
S0.fieldNote: Carla's first reaction to any technology is to ask who it watches, not what it does. She already sees new systems as management tools for timing workers, which shapes how she reads everything after this. Her money is solid and she knows it, so this picture barely touches her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need it in the enterprise agreement, written down, before a single machine goes autonomous. Not a promise from the general manager at a barbecue, a clause. That's what I'd say at work and that's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Underground, robots are already coming. They've got automated loaders on the bottom levels at the mine next door, driven by someone sitting in a room on the surface. I'm good at my job because I can feel the rock through the controls, and that's exactly the thing they'll say a sensor does better. It means my skill stops counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every crew on the delegate list and push for a technology clause in the next agreement: no job losses without retraining paid by the company, and a say in the rollout. I'd keep working and keep saving, I'm not panicking with eight months put away. I won't go learning their software on my own time, though, that's what they want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my rent, but annoyed that the part I'm proud of is the part they want to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never sit in the remote room. What if that's the only seat left on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably sit in it, and hate it for a while. I'd rather be cranky in a chair than gone. But I'd want the chair on the agreement, not handed out as a favour to whoever kisses up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moses, on my crew. He's forty-eight, he's driven loaders his whole life, and he doesn't read well. He'd never get through an online course in remote operation, and nobody would hold his hand.

S1.say: She'd say any automation needs to be written into the enterprise agreement before a single machine goes autonomous. A clause, not a promise from management.
S1.think: She believes her skill comes from feeling the rock through the controls, and she expects the company to say sensors do it better. To her it means her best skill stops counting.
S1.do: Organises delegates to push for a technology clause guaranteeing company-paid retraining and a say in the rollout. Keeps working and saving, but refuses to learn the new software on her own time.
S1.feel: Uneasy and annoyed rather than afraid, because the part of the job she's proud of is the part being targeted.
S1.quote: I'd rather be cranky in a chair than gone.
S1.fieldNote: Her resistance is partly principle: she won't train herself for the company for free. When pushed she'd take the remote chair, so her line is about terms, not refusal. Her worry goes to older crew members like Moses before herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting, honestly. I'd say they've let a handful of tech companies decide what happens to every mining town without asking anyone, and the government should stop it or tax it until it hurts. I'd be at every meeting and I'd be loud online, which isn't really me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm out, and so is everyone I work with. Six months of savings sounds like a lot until you realise there's no other mine to go to, because they'd all have the same robots. The "plenty of jobs nearby" thing is only true while there are humans on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop the deposit. I'd keep the money liquid and cut back hard, no new pickup, no holiday. I'd push the union to demand redundancy at four weeks per year and paid retraining, and I'd sign up to campaign for whoever promises a wage or share for people pushed out. I wouldn't go chasing some coding course, there'd be nothing to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums on the back of a pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long. What does the next month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd have the whole development crew in the crib room, that's the lunch room underground, and we'd write down what we want before management tells us what we get. Two years is the time it takes to negotiate one agreement. They'd have the robots in before we'd finished the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dele that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the house can wait. He'd say nurses will be fine, and I'd tell him nobody is fine in this picture, they're just later on the list. Then we'd probably eat toast for dinner and not talk about it.

S2.say: She'd say a few tech companies have decided the future of mining towns without asking anyone, and government should stop it or tax it hard. She'd be loud at meetings and online, which isn't like her.
S2.think: She thinks she and her whole crew are out, and that her savings and the local job market mean little when every mine has the same robots.
S2.do: Halts the house deposit, keeps savings liquid and cuts spending on a new pickup and holidays. Pushes the union for four weeks' redundancy per year and paid retraining, and campaigns for politicians promising an income or share for displaced workers.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, doing sums at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Two years is the time it takes to negotiate one agreement. They'd have the robots in before we'd finished the meetings.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline breaks the tool she trusts most: slow, collective bargaining. Her strong savings don't comfort her because she sees no other job to move to. She refuses to retrain on principle and also because she sees nothing to retrain for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but with a plan attached. We've got five years to get it in law that the people who dug the profits get a share of the robots. I'd be saying that at the pub, at union, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years still lands me at thirty-two with no trade anyone needs. It's a bit better because the union can actually move in five years. But I'd be watching every new machine come down the decline and counting how many of us it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the union side, delegate to organiser if they'll have me, and work the jumbo as long as there is one. I'd keep saving harder, maybe twenty per cent of each pay. I'd campaign for a law that says mines pay a robot levy into a fund for the towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do with my hands. Having a fight to fight helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change what you'd do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still put the house off, but I wouldn't freeze. Probably pay off my car and keep the rest in the bank. I'm not buying a house in a town that might be empty in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wouldn't learn their software. With five years' warning, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the company pays and it's on shift. I'm stubborn, not stupid. But I'd learn it so I can argue about it properly, not so I can be the one who replaces my crew.

S3.say: She'd say there are five years to get it into law that workers who made the profits share in the robots, and she'd say it at the pub, the union and everywhere else.
S3.think: She expects to be 32 with no trade anyone needs. Five years only helps because the union has time to move.
S3.do: Moves towards full-time union organising while working the jumbo as long as it lasts. Saves about 20 per cent of each pay, pays off her car, and campaigns for a robot levy that pays into a fund for mining towns.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, because having a fight gives her something to do.
S3.quote: I'm not buying a house in a town that might be empty in five years.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter to Carla mainly as organising time, not personal preparation. She softened on learning the new software, but only if the company pays and only to argue about it from the inside. She ties the house decision directly to whether the town survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone left on the scrap heap. If the government does nothing with a decade's warning, that's a choice, and people should vote like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like forever and like no time. I'd still be on the jumbo for most of it, probably. But I know how companies use time: they spend nine years saying it's coming and one year doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving, and keep the union stuff going, but I'd also get properly involved in politics, maybe local council. I'd push for the transition fund early so it's built before it's needed. I wouldn't change jobs yet, there's no point jumping into something that goes the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still. It's a slower worry, the kind that sits in the back of your neck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at thirty-seven. What does that age mean to you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty-seven is when I wanted kids and a house paid down. In the ten-year one I'd be deciding about kids while watching robots learn my job. That's not a small thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start doing this year, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run for the branch committee in the next round. Nobody else my age on site wants it, and if it's coming in ten years, we need people who'll still be around to see it through.

S4.say: She'd say a decade's warning means no excuse for leaving anyone on the scrap heap, and that inaction would be a political choice people should vote on.
S4.think: She thinks companies spend most of the time saying it's coming and then move fast at the end. She expects to stay on the jumbo for most of the decade anyway.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, runs for the union branch committee in the next round, and gets involved in local politics. Pushes for a transition fund to be built early, but doesn't change jobs.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slower, steadier way that sits in the background.
S4.quote: In the ten-year one I'd be deciding about kids while watching robots learn my job.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years doesn't calm her, because she doesn't trust the company to use the time fairly. The decade lands on her plans for children and a house, which makes this personal in a way the faster scenarios weren't. She'd use the time for politics, not a career change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There's no time to organise, and organising is the only thing I know works. What would help is a law that says if a company replaces workers with machines, part of what it saves goes back to those workers and their town, for years, not a one-off cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. The company will say robots are safer underground, and in some ways they are, I've pulled a mate out from under a rock fall. I'm not against safer. I'm against them using safety as the reason, when the real reason is the wage bill.

headlineQuote: I'm good at my job because I can feel the rock through the controls, and that's exactly the thing they'll say a sensor does better.
portrait: Carla Mensah is 27 and leads a development crew underground at a gold mine, running a twin-boom jumbo drill nine hundred metres down. She lives with her partner Dele, a nurse, has more than six months saved, and is a union delegate who distrusts every new system the company brings in. In the mild picture she is calm and a little smug; in Steady Disruption she turns to the enterprise agreement. In the AGI pictures she is alarmed by two years, anxious with five or ten, and in every case she reaches for collective bargaining and politics rather than retraining on her own time.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to organise, and organising is the only thing she trusts to work.
whatWouldHelp: A law that sends part of what companies save by replacing workers back to those workers and their town, for years rather than as a one-off payment.
